386.title: Arousing
386.hook: waking good states not yet present
386.howItsDone: Buddhists cultivate wholesome qualities through daily practices such as meditation, chanting, generosity and keeping good company; teachers often stress the spiritual friend, kalyāṇamitta.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abandoning, and your line, a finer peg. When a sticky thought came back, did a better peg push it through? Day three hundred eighty-six.

Patience with small children. Giving without keeping score. Staying calm when the flight is canceled and the line at the desk is shouting. They're the qualities people admire in a friend and wish they had. Qualities like these are easy to file under personality: some people got them, some didn't. The suttas file them somewhere else. The third of the four efforts is about exactly this: bringing into being good qualities that aren't there yet. Today: arousing.
screen: `PATIENT WITH SMALL CHILDREN.` → `CALM AT THE CANCELED FLIGHT.` → `PERSONALITY, OR PRACTICE?`

segments.voice: The text is short: for wholesome states that haven't arisen, one generates desire, makes an effort, rouses energy, and strives for them to arise. Notice the first step is desire, chanda: the wish to have the good thing. Buddhism is sometimes summed up as wanting nothing at all. The suttas are more careful. Wanting to grow in kindness or patience isn't the problem; it's the fuel. In the next sutta over, the Buddha says what this effort develops: the seven factors of awakening, mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration and equanimity. So how do good states get started? The Book of Ones, the first section of the Numbered Discourses, keeps coming back to two sparks. One is wise attention: turning the mind toward things in a way that wakes the good. The other is good friendship: spending time with people who already have it. That's practical. You don't grow patience by staring at the word. You grow it by noticing the small moments where patience is possible, and by being around patient people until it rubs off. Then there's the honest obstacle: inertia. The Dhammapada names it plainly, in Max Müller's words: "He who does not rouse himself when it is time to rise" will not find the way. Arousing the good is mostly about starting, small and on a specific day. The first patient minute happens on one particular morning.
screen: `GOOD QUALITIES CAN BE GROWN.` · `CHANDA: THE WISH IS THE FUEL.` · `TWO SPARKS: ATTENTION AND FRIENDS.` · `A HABIT BEGINS AS ONE MORNING.` · then, large: `WAKE THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Choose one good quality you'd like more of: patience, generosity, courage, steadiness. Remember one moment, even a tiny one, when you had a little of it. Let that moment come back in detail: where you were, how it felt in the body. That's wise attention, turning toward the seed. Then choose the smallest possible way to practice it today, and picture yourself doing it once. The bell holds the time.
Arousing. The third effort: bringing good states into being. The wish for the good, wise attention, and good friends are the sparks.
Your line: wake the good. Today, start one good habit, as small as you like, and do it once. Day three hundred eighty-six.

387.title: Maintaining
387.hook: keeping good states going and growing
387.howItsDone: Buddhist practitioners keep daily routines, a morning sit, evening chanting, regular offerings, and many traditions encourage rejoicing in one's own good deeds as a way of sustaining them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arousing, and your line, wake the good. Did you start one good habit, and do it once? Day three hundred eighty-seven.

Day one of a new habit has the thrill of starting. Day two is just doing it again. No fanfare, no new pen. A beautiful journal gets three lovely pages, and six months later it turns up under the bed, the rest of it blank. Starting a good thing is the third effort. Keeping it going is the fourth, and for this one the Buddha reached for pictures from the farmyard and the workshop. Today: maintaining.
screen: `DAY ONE: THE THRILL.` → `DAY TWO: AGAIN.` → `THE JOURNAL UNDER THE BED.`

segments.voice: The fourth effort, in the Numbered Discourses, is for wholesome states that have already arisen: you work to keep them, so they don't fade or get muddled, and to help them grow and come to fullness. The Pali name is anurakkhaṇā, protecting, guarding what you have. In the list's own example, it's a meditator protecting a steady object of concentration once they've found it. But how do you keep at something without straining? A sutta in the Connected Discourses gives two pictures. A hen sits on her eggs, eight or ten or twelve. She covers them, warms them, tends them properly. She doesn't need to wish, may my chicks break out today. If she keeps sitting, they will. Then a carpenter looks at the handle of his adze, a woodworking tool, and sees the marks his fingers have worn into it. He couldn't tell you how much wore away today, or yesterday. But it wore. Practice is like that, the Buddha says: a monk can't see how much of the mind's taints wore away today, but steady practice wears them away. That's the spirit of maintaining. Not dramatic. Not checking every hour. Just sitting on the eggs. The Dhammapada adds the other half, in Max Müller's words: "If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good." Do it again, and enjoy it. Gladness isn't a distraction from keeping a good thing going. It's part of what keeps it going.
screen: `ANURAKKHAṆĀ: GUARDING WHAT'S GROWN.` · `THE HEN ON HER EGGS.` · `THE WORN ADZE HANDLE.` · `DO IT AGAIN, AND ENJOY IT.` · then, large: `KEEP IT GOING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring back the good habit you started yesterday, or any good thing you've been doing lately. Don't measure it. Don't ask whether it's working. Just picture yourself doing it again today, the way a hen settles back onto her eggs: no fuss, no wishing, simply returning. Let a little gladness come with the picture, if it wants to. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Maintaining. Anurakkhaṇā, the fourth effort: keeping good states going and growing, like a hen sitting on her eggs.
Your line: keep it going. Today, continue yesterday's good once more, and let yourself enjoy it. Day three hundred eighty-seven.

388.title: The lute string
388.hook: Sona strains too hard; the Buddha asks how a lute sounds when its strings are too tight or too loose (AN 6.55)
388.howItsDone: Meditation teachers across Buddhist traditions tell Sona's story to students who push too hard or drift, and encourage them to adjust effort through a sit rather than force it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: maintaining, and your line, keep it going. Did yesterday's good get done once more, and did you enjoy it? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

On the walking path in a forest called the Cool Grove, a young monk has been pacing back and forth for so long that his feet are bleeding. The path behind him is stained. His name is Sona. He grew up wealthy and sheltered, and he has decided to make up for it by trying harder than anyone else. And right in the middle of all that effort, he's thinking about quitting. On day twenty you met the image at the heart of this story. Today, the whole story: the lute string.
screen: `THE COOL GROVE.` → `PACING UNTIL HIS FEET BLEED.` → `THINKING OF QUITTING.`

segments.voice: Sona's thought, the sutta says, runs like this. I'm one of the most energetic of the Buddha's disciples, and still my mind isn't free. My family has wealth. I could go home, enjoy it, and do good with it. The Buddha knows what he's thinking and comes to him. He doesn't scold, and he doesn't push. He asks about music. Sona, before you went forth, weren't you skilled at the lute? Yes, sir. When its strings were too tight, did it sound right? No, sir. When they were too loose? No, sir. And when they were neither too tight nor too loose, tuned to an even pitch? Then it sounded right, sir. In the same way, the Buddha says, effort that's too strong leads to restlessness, and effort that's too slack leads to laziness. So settle on an even pitch of effort, and tune the rest of your practice to it. The vīṇā, the Indian lute, isn't a random choice. Sona knows it with his hands. The Buddha teaches him in the language of his own skill. That matters for the four efforts we've just walked through. Effort isn't a dial that only turns up. Some days the string is slack, and you need to rouse yourself. Some days it's wound so tight it buzzes, and you need to ease off. The sutta says Sona took this to heart, practiced with balance, and before long became an arahant, fully awakened. The walking path stayed the same. The tuning changed.
screen: `TRYING HARDER THAN ANYONE.` · `TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE.` · `THE EVEN PITCH OF EFFORT.` · `EASE OFF, OR TURN IT UP.` · then, large: `TUNE THE STRING.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and check the string. Is your body tight right now, jaw set, shoulders up, trying to meditate correctly? Then ease it a quarter turn, and let the breath happen. Or is it slack, drifting, half asleep? Then tighten a little: sit up, and feel the breath more clearly. Keep tuning gently through the sit, a little looser, a little tighter, listening for the even note. The bell holds the time.
Vina, the Indian lute. The Buddha's lesson for Sona: effort too tight brings restlessness, too loose brings laziness. Tune it to an even pitch.
Your line: tune the string. Today, find one place you're straining and ease it, or one place you've gone slack and tighten it, just one turn. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

389.title: Right mindfulness
389.hook: the four foundations, now as a factor of the path (MN 141)
389.howItsDone: Buddhists practice right mindfulness through satipaṭṭhāna meditation, often beginning with the breath, and through attention carried into daily activity; in Theravada the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta is widely chanted and studied.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vina, and your line, tune the string. Where did you ease off, or tighten up, by one turn? Day three hundred eighty-nine.

In the Deer Park near Benares, where he first taught, the Buddha gives his monks a brief summary of the four noble truths. Then he praises Sariputta and Moggallana, says Sariputta can explain the truths in detail, gets up, and goes into his dwelling. It's one of the moments the canon records him handing the teaching to a student. Sariputta takes it from there, truth by truth, factor by factor. And when he reaches the seventh factor of the path, he defines it in one long, careful sentence. Today: right mindfulness.
screen: `THE DEER PARK, AGAIN.` → `A BRIEF SUMMARY.` → `SARIPUTTA TAKES IT FROM THERE.`

segments.voice: Sammā sati. Sati is usually translated mindfulness, but it corresponds to the Sanskrit smṛti, memory. So mindfulness here is less like a spotlight and more like remembering: remembering to notice, remembering what you're doing while you're doing it. Sariputta's sentence goes like this. A practitioner dwells contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly knowing, and mindful, having set aside wanting and grief about the world. Then feelings as feelings. The mind as mind. And dhammas, the patterns of experience, as dhammas. Four foundations. They may sound familiar: the first year spent three weeks on them. What's new today is where they sit. On their own, they're a meditation method. As the seventh factor of the path, they're a working part of something larger. Right view tells mindfulness what to look for. Right effort supplies the energy to keep looking. Right concentration, later on the path, gathers what mindfulness has noticed into stillness. And remember the great forty sutta, where three factors circle around each of the others? Mindfulness is one of the three. It's there inside right speech, right action, right livelihood, all of it. That's why the line is so plain: remember to notice. Not a special state you visit on a cushion. A habit of remembering, in the middle of an ordinary day, that you're here, in a body, feeling something, thinking something, and that you can see it.
screen: `SATI: ROOTED IN MEMORY.` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `A WORKING PART OF THE PATH.` · `REMEMBERING THAT YOU'RE HERE.` · then, large: `REMEMBER TO NOTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let's touch all four foundations, about half a minute each. First the body: where it meets the seat, its weight, the breath moving. Then feeling: is this moment pleasant, unpleasant, or neither? Just know it. Then the mind: calm, restless, sleepy, bright? Then whatever pattern is here: a wanting, a pushing away, some ease. Each time you drift, that's fine. Remembering is the practice. The bell holds the time, and if you have five minutes afterward, stay.
Sammā sati. Right mindfulness: the four foundations, body, feelings, mind and dhammas, as the seventh factor of the path.
Your line: remember to notice. Today, each time you walk through a doorway, remember: body, feeling, mind. Day three hundred eighty-nine.

smṛti: mindfulness is remembering to notice.

fork.reveal: in MN 141 the Buddha rises and enters his dwelling, and Sariputta analyzes the four truths, including each factor of the path.

original.note: Pali sammā sati: right mindfulness, the seventh factor of the eightfold path; sati corresponds to Sanskrit smṛti, memory.

trapdoor: what you thought: mindfulness is a relaxation technique.
what it means: remembering to notice body, feelings, mind and dhammas, as one working factor of the path.
what a scholar hears: Pali sati corresponds to Sanskrit smṛti; MN 141 defines right mindfulness with the full satipaṭṭhāna formula, and MN 117 makes it one of three factors that circle every other.

390.title: The gatekeeper
390.hook: mindfulness is like the wise gatekeeper of a frontier fortress (AN 7, the fortress)
390.howItsDone: Meditation teachers often use the gatekeeper image to describe mindfulness as noticing and naming what arises, and some traditions practice mental noting, labeling each thought or feeling as it appears.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma sati, right mindfulness, and your line, remember to notice. Did a doorway remind you once: body, feeling, mind? Day three hundred ninety.

At the edge of a kingdom, where the road comes in from foreign land, stands a fortress. Thick walls. A moat. Soldiers. Storerooms of grain and oil. And at the gate, one person whose whole job is to look at every face that arrives and decide: you, come in; you, I don't know you, wait outside. Everything inside depends on that one person paying attention. The Buddha drew this fortress in detail, piece by piece. Today: the gatekeeper.
screen: `A FORTRESS ON THE FRONTIER.` → `WALLS, MOAT, SOLDIERS, STORES.` → `ONE PERSON AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: The sutta is in the book of sevens of the Numbered Discourses. A king's frontier fortress, the Buddha says, can't be taken by enemies from outside when it has seven things in place and four kinds of provisions stored. Then he maps each piece onto a practitioner. The deep-rooted pillar at the entrance is faith. The moat is a sense of shame about doing wrong. The path patrolled around the walls is fear of wrongdoing. The weapons are learning, the teachings you've heard. The army is energy. The high, thick rampart is wisdom. And the gatekeeper, wise, experienced and intelligent, who keeps strangers out and lets known friends in, is mindfulness. Notice what the gatekeeper does and doesn't do. He doesn't fight; that's the army's job. He doesn't build the walls. He knows who's who, and he's at his post. Mindfulness, in this picture, is what recognizes what's arriving. That's anger, coming up the road. That's kindness, a friend: open the gate. Without the gatekeeper, the strongest walls are useless. The enemy simply walks in, because no one noticed. A few days ago you guarded the sense doors. This is the same gate, seen from inside the walls, and it echoes a Dhammapada line from the first year, in Max Müller's words: "Like a well-guarded frontier fort, with defences within and without, so let a man guard himself." A frontier fort, not a palace. Mindfulness stands where ordinary life arrives.
screen: `SEVEN DEFENSES, FOUR STORES.` · `PILLAR, MOAT, WEAPONS, ARMY, WALL.` · `THE GATEKEEPER KNOWS WHO'S WHO.` · `WHERE ORDINARY LIFE ARRIVES.` · then, large: `THE GATEKEEPER.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and picture yourself at the gate. Thoughts and moods come up the road, one at a time. As each one arrives, just name it, the way a gatekeeper would: worry. Planning. A memory. Irritation. Tenderness. Don't fight any of them. Just recognize them. If you like, let the friendly ones in, and let the strangers wait outside. Your only job is to stay at your post. The bell holds the time.
The gatekeeper. In the book of sevens, mindfulness is the wise gatekeeper of the frontier fortress, the one who knows who's who.
Your line: know who's who. Today, be your own gatekeeper: when a mood arrives, name it before you let it in. Day three hundred ninety.

391.title: The bowl of oil
391.hook: carry a full bowl of oil past a crowd and a dancing beauty, a swordsman behind you (SN 47.20)
391.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body in walking meditation and daily tasks, and some teachers have students carry a full cup or bowl slowly as a training in steady attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gatekeeper, and your line, know who's who. When a mood arrived, did you name it before you let it in? Day three hundred ninety-one.

A huge crowd is gathering in the town square. Word has spread: the most beautiful woman in the land is here, and she's dancing and singing. People are pushing to see. Now a man is handed a bowl filled to the very brim with oil, and told to carry it straight through the middle of all that, between the crowd and the dancer. Behind him walks another man, with a drawn sword. Spill one drop, he's told, and you lose your head. Today: the bowl of oil.
screen: `THE CROWD PUSHES TO SEE.` → `A BOWL FULL TO THE BRIM.` → `A DRAWN SWORD BEHIND.`

segments.voice: The Buddha tells this at Sedaka, the same town as the acrobats. And he asks his monks a simple question. Would that man stop paying attention to the bowl, and let his eyes drift to the dancer? No, sir, they say. Of course not. Then the Buddha says what the picture means. The bowl of oil filled to the brim stands for mindfulness of the body. So train yourselves, he says, to develop mindfulness of the body, to make it your vehicle and your ground. The picture is extreme on purpose, and each piece is worth a look. The crowd and the dancer are everything that pulls attention outward: the alerts, the drama, the bright, loud, lovely things. The sutta doesn't explain the sword, but one way to read it is as the seriousness of the stakes. Not that distraction is a crime; just that it may cost more than we tend to think. And the bowl is the body itself: the breath, the feet, the hands, right here. Not something far away. The thing you're already carrying. Notice what the man doesn't do. He doesn't shut his eyes. He doesn't stay home. He walks straight through the crowd while the music plays. The practice isn't avoiding life. It's carrying something steady through the middle of it. That's right mindfulness at its most physical. Attention isn't floating somewhere up in the head. It's in your hands, at the brim of the bowl, step by step, while everything around you invites you to look away.
screen: `WOULD HE LOOK AWAY?` · `THE BOWL: MINDFULNESS OF THE BODY.` · `THE SWORD: THE STAKES ARE REAL.` · `THROUGH THE CROWD, NOT AROUND IT.` · then, large: `DON'T SPILL.`

segments.voice: If you can, fill a cup or glass with water, right to the top, and hold it. If not, imagine one in your hands. Feel its weight. Now, slowly, carry it a few steps, or simply raise it and lower it, without spilling. Notice how the whole body gathers around the brim: the breath slows, the hands soften, the eyes stay close. That's the bowl of oil. Then set it down and sit, feeling the same steadiness in the body. The bell holds the time.
Kayagata sati, mindfulness of the body. The Buddha's image for mindfulness of the body: carried brim-full through the crowd, without spilling.
Your line: don't spill. Today, carry one full cup slowly, through your kitchen or your office, and let the rest of the room wait. Day three hundred ninety-one.

392.title: Six animals
392.hook: a snake, crocodile, bird, dog, jackal and monkey tied to one post: the body as the post (SN 35.247)
392.howItsDone: Many Buddhists practice mindfulness of the body by returning attention to posture and breath through the day, in walking as well as sitting meditation; teachers in several schools describe the body as an anchor for the wandering mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kayagata sati, and your line, don't spill. Did you carry one full cup slowly, and notice how the whole body had to pay attention? Day three hundred ninety-two, the end of the week.

A man walks into a clearing with six animals on six ropes. A snake. A crocodile. A bird. A dog. A jackal. A monkey. He knots the six ropes together in the middle, and lets go. You can guess what happens next. The snake heads for its anthill. The crocodile heads for the river. The bird heads for the sky, the dog for the village, the jackal for the charnel ground, the monkey for the forest. Six directions, one knot, and whoever is strongest drags the rest. If you've ever opened your phone to check one thing and surfaced forty minutes later, you've met this knot. Today: the six animals, and the post.
screen: `SIX ANIMALS, SIX ROPES.` → `SIX DIRECTIONS, ONE KNOT.` → `THE STRONGEST DRAGS THE REST.`

segments.voice: The story comes from the Connected Discourses, in the book on the six senses. The Buddha tells it twice. The first time, the ropes are only tied to each other. Each animal pulls toward its own place, and the others get dragged after whichever is strongest. Then he tells it again with a single change. This time the man ties all six ropes to a strong post, driven deep into the ground. The animals pull just as hard. The snake still wants its anthill. The monkey still wants its forest. Nobody has been tamed. But the post doesn't move. And after a while, worn out, they stand by the post, then sit down by it, then lie down beside it. Then he explains. The six animals are the six senses: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, each pulling toward what it likes and away from what it doesn't. The post is mindfulness directed to the body, kayagata sati in Pali: knowing you're sitting while you sit, knowing you're breathing while you breathe. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say kill the animals, or blindfold the eye, or stop up the ear. The senses keep their nature. The snake is still a snake. What changes is that there's something steady for all of them to be tied to. That's why this story belongs under right mindfulness, the seventh factor of the path. Mindfulness here isn't a mood. It's a post. Some teachers put it this way: the body is always here, and it's the mind that runs off to the anthill and the forest. Coming back to the feet on the floor is coming back to the post. And it's the end of a week: waking the good, keeping it going, the lute string tuned, remembering to notice, the gatekeeper, the bowl of oil, and today, six animals with something to be tied to.

segments.voice: Sit, and find the post first. Feel your feet, the weight of your body on the seat, your hands where they rest. Then let the animals pull. A sound will tug at the ear. A thought will drag toward tomorrow. An itch will call from somewhere. You don't have to stop any of them. Just notice which one is pulling, and come back to the weight of the body. A pull, and back to the post. Another pull, and back. By the end, some of them may be lying down. The bell holds the time.
Six animals. The six senses, each pulling toward its own place, tied to one steady post: mindfulness of the body.
Your line: the post holds. Today, when something drags your attention away, feel your feet on the ground for one breath before you follow it. Day three hundred ninety-two.

fork.setup: you've tied six animals to a strong post driven deep into the ground. they pull in six directions. what happens, in the Buddha's story?
options: the post breaks
they pull, tire, and lie down beside the post
the strongest drags the others away
fork.reveal: the post doesn't move. worn out, the animals stand, then sit, then lie down beside it. the senses aren't destroyed; they're given something steady.

original.note: Pali saḷāyatana: the six sense bases, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, which the six animals stand for.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of animals to make a point about distraction.
what it means: six senses, each with its own pull, and one steady post that lets them settle.

what a scholar hears: the post is named kāyagatā sati, mindfulness directed to the body; the sutta is numbered SN 35.247 in Bhikkhu Bodhi's edition and SN 35.206 in the older Pali Text Society numbering.
